questions.stem: Which is the best research question for an investigation?
options: Is the creek near the mine site nice to swim in during summer?
What do people in the town think about the old mine site?
Why is mining good for the local economy of the region?
How does distance from a mine site affect the pH of creek water?
questions.explanation: A good research question names measurable variables (distance and pH) and can be answered with data. The other questions rely on opinion or are not testable by a scientific investigation.

questions.stem: Which hypothesis is written in a testable form?
options: Soil organic content and moisture are both interesting properties to measure in a lab
If soil organic content increases, then its moisture content after drying for 24 hours will increase
Soil is very important to plants and animals, so it should always be looked after carefully
Some soils might be better than others, depending on many different things in the garden
questions.explanation: A testable hypothesis predicts a relationship between an independent and a dependent variable that data could support or refute. The other statements are value judgements or too vague to test.

questions.stem: Students measure the number of mangrove seedlings at sites with different distances from a boat ramp, without changing any conditions themselves. Which type of investigation is this?
options: Descriptive
Secondary data
Correlational
Experimental
questions.explanation: A correlational investigation looks for a relationship between two measured variables without the investigator manipulating either. An experiment would require the students to deliberately change the independent variable.

questions.stem: Students compare the mean grain size of sand from a sheltered beach with that from an exposed surf beach. Which type of investigation is this?
options: Correlational
Experimental
Descriptive
Comparative
questions.explanation: A comparative investigation compares a variable between two or more groups or sites, here grain size at two beaches. A correlational study would measure a continuous variable, such as wave height, at many sites.

questions.stem: A student analyses 30 years of Bureau of Meteorology rainfall records to test whether El Niño years are drier in Brisbane. What type of investigation is this?
options: Experimental investigation
Descriptive field investigation
Laboratory model investigation
Secondary data investigation
questions.explanation: The student is analysing data collected by others, which is a secondary data investigation. No variables are manipulated and no new primary data are collected.

questions.stem: In an experiment on how water temperature affects the rate at which calcium carbonate dissolves in acid, which variable is the dependent variable?
options: The mass of calcium carbonate added at the start
The rate at which the calcium carbonate dissolves
The temperature of the water in each beaker
The volume and concentration of acid used
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the one measured in response to changes in the independent variable, here the dissolving rate. Temperature is the independent variable, and acid volume, concentration and mass are controlled variables.

questions.stem: Students find that sites with more leaf litter have more invertebrates. However, the leafier sites were also shadier and damper. What is the best evaluation?
options: Leaf litter must be the cause, because a correlation between two variables always shows causation
Shade and moisture are dependent variables, so they should have been plotted on the vertical axis
The result is invalid, because invertebrates cannot be counted reliably in any field investigation
Shade and moisture are confounding variables, so leaf litter alone cannot be shown to cause the difference
questions.explanation: A confounding variable changes along with the independent variable and could explain the result. Because shade and moisture varied with leaf litter, the study cannot attribute the difference to leaf litter alone. Correlation does not by itself show causation.

questions.stem: Why do scientists use replicates and adequate sample sizes in an investigation?
options: To avoid needing a control in an experimental investigation
To reduce the effect of random variation and give more reliable results
To remove systematic errors caused by a badly calibrated instrument
To make the results agree with the hypothesis that was proposed
questions.explanation: Repeating trials and sampling more sites averages out random variation, giving more reliable results. Replicates do not remove systematic error, which shifts every reading the same way, and they never replace a control.

questions.stem: Students survey vegetation across a coastal dune from the beach to the forest. Which sampling technique is most appropriate?
options: A belt transect with quadrats at regular intervals from the beach inland
Ten quadrats placed randomly in the middle of the forest only
A single quadrat at the top of the highest dune in the system
Mark and recapture of plants along the edge of the beach
questions.explanation: A transect runs across the environmental gradient, so quadrats along it show how species change with distance from the sea. Random quadrats in one zone cannot show change, and mark and recapture is used for mobile animals.

questions.stem: Before measuring pH in a creek, a student checks the pH meter in buffer solutions of known pH 4.0 and 7.0 and adjusts it. What is the purpose of this step?
options: To remove random error caused by changes in the creek
To control the temperature of the creek water sampled
To calibrate the meter so that its readings are accurate
To make the readings more precise by repeating them
questions.explanation: Calibration against standards of known value corrects systematic error, so readings are accurate. It does not remove random variation in the creek, and it does not control temperature.

questions.stem: A student estimates percentage cover of grass in quadrats by eye, and a classmate estimates the same quadrats 15% higher every time. What type of error does this suggest, and how could it be reduced?
options: A systematic error in the grass, reduced by choosing quadrats that contain less grass
A systematic error between observers, reduced by using a grid quadrat and one trained observer
A random error between observers, reduced by having each student repeat the same estimate twice
A random error in the grass, reduced by sampling the same quadrats on a different day
questions.explanation: A consistent difference in one direction is a systematic error, here caused by observer bias. A gridded quadrat with counted squares and using one trained observer makes estimates more objective. Repeating biased estimates does not remove the bias.

questions.stem: Which describes a random error?
options: A difference between two variables that is caused by a third variable
Unpredictable variation that scatters readings above and below the true value
A consistent shift that makes every reading too high by the same amount
A mistake in copying numbers from a field notebook into a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Random errors cause readings to scatter unpredictably around the true value and are reduced by repeating measurements and averaging. A consistent shift is a systematic error, and a copying slip is a personal mistake.

questions.stem: A balance reads 0.3 g when nothing is on it, and the student does not notice. How will this affect the soil masses recorded?
options: Every mass will scatter randomly by up to 0.3 g, a random error that reduces precision
Only the first mass will be wrong, because the balance corrects itself afterwards
No mass will be affected, because the error is too small to matter in soil work
Every mass will be 0.3 g too high, a systematic error that reduces accuracy
questions.explanation: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount, so it is systematic and makes results inaccurate, though they may still be precise. It can be corrected by taring the balance or subtracting 0.3 g.

questions.stem: Repeated measurements of nitrate in one water sample are 2.1, 2.2, 2.1 and 2.2 mg/L. The true value is 3.0 mg/L. How are these results best described?
options: Neither accurate nor precise
Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
questions.explanation: The readings are close to each other, so they are precise, but they are all far from the true value, so they are not accurate. This pattern points to a systematic error.

questions.stem: Three readings of water temperature are 18.2, 18.6 and 18.4 °C. Using the mean and half the range as the uncertainty, how should the result be recorded?
questions.explanation: The mean is (18.2 + 18.6 + 18.4) ÷ 3 = 18.4 °C. The range is 18.6 − 18.2 = 0.4 °C, so half the range is 0.2 °C. Using the full range overstates the uncertainty under this convention.

questions.stem: A soil sample's mass is 25.0 ± 0.5 g. What is the percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ measured value × 100 = 0.5 ÷ 25.0 × 100 = 2%. The value 0.02 is the fraction before multiplying by 100.

questions.stem: Students measure dissolved oxygen as 6.9 mg/L, while a calibrated reference instrument gives 7.5 mg/L. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |6.9 − 7.5| ÷ 7.5 × 100 = 0.6 ÷ 7.5 × 100 = 8%. Dividing by the student's value instead gives about 8.7%, and 0.6 is the absolute difference, not a percentage.

questions.stem: The standard deviation of a data set describes:
options: The value that occurs most often in the data set
How close the mean is to the true population value
How spread out the values are around the mean
The difference between the largest and smallest value
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures the typical spread of data values around the mean; a small value means data are clustered closely. The difference between extremes is the range, and the most frequent value is the mode.

questions.stem: A sample of 25 soil cores has a mean organic content of 6.0% and a standard deviation of 1.5%. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: Standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n = 1.5 ÷ √25 = 1.5 ÷ 5 = 0.3%. Dividing by n instead of √n gives 0.06%. The standard error describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean.

questions.stem: A Student's t-test comparing invertebrate counts at two creek sites gives p = 0.01. Using the usual significance level of 0.05, what can be concluded?
options: The difference between the site means is statistically significant
The difference between the site means is due only to chance
The two sites have exactly the same mean invertebrate count
The test proves which site has the healthier ecosystem
questions.explanation: A p-value below 0.05 means a difference this large would be unlikely if there were no real difference, so it is statistically significant. It does not prove a cause or which site is healthier, and the means are clearly not identical.

questions.stem: Mean seedling counts at two sites are plotted as columns with standard error bars. The error bars overlap widely. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The difference between the means is significant, because the columns have different heights
The data are invalid, because error bars should never overlap in a well-designed study
The site with the taller column definitely has more seedlings across the whole region
The difference between the means is unlikely to be significant, so more data or a test is needed
questions.explanation: Widely overlapping standard error bars suggest the difference could be due to sampling variation, so it is unlikely to be significant. A statistical test or larger samples would be needed to decide. Overlap does not make data invalid.

questions.stem: A scatterplot of tree density against soil moisture across 20 sites gives Pearson's correlation coefficient r = −0.85. What does this indicate?
options: No correlation, because negative values of r mean the data are unreliable
A strong negative correlation: tree density tends to fall as soil moisture rises
A weak negative correlation: tree density hardly changes as soil moisture rises
A strong positive correlation: tree density tends to rise as soil moisture rises
questions.explanation: Pearson's r ranges from −1 to +1. A value of −0.85 is close to −1, showing a strong negative linear relationship. The sign shows direction, and the size shows strength.

questions.stem: A trendline fitted to a scatterplot of stream temperature against riparian shade has R² = 0.64. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The trendline passes through 64% of the data points plotted on the graph
The correlation coefficient r is 0.64, so the relationship is weak
About 64% of the variation in stream temperature is explained by the trendline
Shade causes 64% of the warming of streams across Queensland in every season
questions.explanation: R² is the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the fitted line. It does not show cause, and it is not the fraction of points on the line. Here r would be about ±0.8, since R² = r².

questions.stem: A creek's phosphate concentration is 0.045 mg/L. What is this in µg/L?
options: 450 µg/L
45 µg/L
4.5 µg/L
questions.explanation: There are 1000 µg in 1 mg, so 0.045 mg/L × 1000 = 45 µg/L. Converting from a larger unit to a smaller unit makes the number bigger, not smaller.

questions.stem: A survey area of mangrove forest is 0.35 km². What is this area in hectares?
options: 350 ha
35 ha
3.5 ha
questions.explanation: One square kilometre is 100 hectares (1 km² = 1 000 000 m², and 1 ha = 10 000 m²). So 0.35 km² × 100 = 35 ha.

questions.stem: Which graph is most suitable for showing the relationship between two continuous variables, such as rainfall and stream flow measured at 30 sites?
options: A table of the stream flow only
A scatterplot with a trendline
A pie chart of the rainfall values
A column graph of the site names
questions.explanation: A scatterplot shows how one continuous variable changes with another, and a trendline summarises the relationship. Column graphs suit comparisons between categories, and pie charts show parts of a whole.

questions.stem: Which representation best shows how vegetation and elevation change along a transect from a beach across a dune system?
options: A summary table giving only the mean height of all plants combined
A profile diagram showing the ground surface with plants drawn at each position
A pie chart showing the percentage of each plant species in the whole area
A scatterplot of species name against the date on which it was recorded
questions.explanation: A profile diagram shows the shape of the land along the transect with the vegetation at each point, making zonation easy to see. A pie chart or a single mean loses all information about position.

questions.stem: Data from 2000 to 2020 show a steady rise in sea level at a tide gauge. A student uses the trendline to estimate the level in 2040. What is this called, and what is its main risk?
options: Interpolation; it assumes the data inside the measured range contain no errors
Calibration; it assumes the tide gauge was correctly set up at the start
Replication; it assumes the measurements were repeated at every tide gauge
Extrapolation; it assumes the trend continues unchanged beyond the measured range
questions.explanation: Estimating beyond the range of measured data is extrapolation. It assumes the same relationship holds into the future, which may not be true if the rate changes. Interpolation estimates values within the data range.

questions.stem: A student's hypothesis was that grazing reduces soil organic content. Mean values were 4.1% (grazed) and 4.3% (ungrazed) from three samples each, with large standard deviations. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The hypothesis is proven, because the grazed mean is lower than the ungrazed mean
The hypothesis is disproven, because the difference between the means is small
The hypothesis should be changed so that it matches the data that were collected
The data do not provide strong evidence for the hypothesis; more samples are needed
questions.explanation: A small difference between means with few samples and large variation is not strong evidence either way. The appropriate response is to state the limitation and collect more data. A hypothesis is never proven by one data set, nor changed to fit results afterwards.

questions.stem: Which change would most improve the validity of an experiment testing whether salinity affects the growth of mangrove seedlings?
options: Repeating the whole experiment the following year with the same method and equipment
Using a more expensive ruler made by a well-known scientific supply company
Keeping light, temperature and soil the same for all seedlings so only salinity differs
Measuring the seedlings' height to the nearest millimetre rather than the nearest centimetre
questions.explanation: Validity is about whether the investigation actually tests what it claims to. Controlling other variables ensures any growth difference is due to salinity. Finer measurements improve precision, and repeating tests reliability.

questions.stem: Two student groups use the same method to measure the turbidity of a dam and obtain very similar results. What does this mainly show?
options: The method is biased, because both groups had the same results
The method is reliable, because it gives consistent results when repeated
The method is accurate, because both groups must have found the true value
The method is valid, because the dam water is the independent variable
questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency when a measurement is repeated. Agreement between groups does not guarantee accuracy, since both could share a systematic error in the method or instrument.

questions.stem: A student finds two online sources about coal seam gas and groundwater. One is a peer-reviewed university study; the other is a company's advertising brochure. How should the sources be evaluated?
options: Reject both, because no source about a contested environmental issue can be trusted at all
Weigh authorship, review process and bias; the peer-reviewed study is generally more reliable
Treat both sources equally, because any information published online has been checked by experts
Prefer the brochure, because companies have the most direct knowledge of their own operations
questions.explanation: Evaluating sources means considering who wrote them, whether they were reviewed, their purpose and possible bias. Peer review and independence make the university study generally more credible, though it should still be read critically. A brochure has a commercial purpose.

questions.stem: A class's measured value for the density of a basalt sample is well below published values. Which is the best next step?
options: Change the published value in the report so that it matches the class's measurement
Ignore the published values, because class measurements are always more reliable
Repeat the calculation using a different answer until it matches the textbook
Compare the method with the expected value and look for sources of error, such as air bubbles
questions.explanation: Comparing results with accepted values helps identify errors in the method, such as trapped air when measuring volume by displacement. Results should be reported honestly, and the procedure improved to reduce uncertainty.

questions.stem: Before using dilute hydrochloric acid to test rocks for carbonate, which document should students consult for hazards, safe handling and first aid?
options: The safety data sheet (SDS) for the chemical
The geological map of the local area
The rock classification key or flow chart
The logbook from the last field trip
questions.explanation: A safety data sheet, also called a material safety data sheet, gives a chemical's hazards, safe handling, storage, disposal and first aid. Maps, keys and logbooks do not contain this information.

questions.stem: Students collecting water samples from a creek identify the risk of slipping on wet rocks. Which control measure best reduces this risk?
options: Sampling only on hot days, when rocks are less likely to be wet
Asking a classmate to watch, without changing how or where the sample is taken
Sampling from a stable bank with a sampling pole, in enclosed shoes with good grip
Sampling quickly so that less time is spent standing near the water's edge
questions.explanation: The most effective controls reduce exposure to the hazard, such as staying on a stable bank and using a pole, combined with suitable footwear. Rushing can increase the risk, and simply watching does not reduce it.

questions.stem: Which action best minimises the environmental impact of a soil survey in a national park?
options: Digging deep pits at many random sites so that the data set is as large as possible
Clearing vegetation from each site so that soil can be sampled more easily
Collecting plants with the soil samples to identify them later in the classroom
Obtaining permission, taking only small samples and refilling holes before leaving
questions.explanation: Ethical fieldwork minimises disturbance: permits, small samples and restoring sites protect the environment. Clearing vegetation or removing plants causes avoidable harm and may be illegal in a national park.

questions.stem: Why must scientists acknowledge their sources and use a standard referencing convention?
options: To show that all of the ideas in the report are the writer's own
To avoid having to explain any of the evidence in their own words
To credit others' work and let readers locate and check the sources
To make a report longer so that it appears to contain more research
questions.explanation: Referencing credits the original authors, avoids plagiarism and lets readers find and evaluate the evidence. It does not replace explaining and analysing the evidence in one's own words.

questions.stem: Why should students record raw data, observations and any changes to the procedure in a logbook during an investigation?
options: It replaces the need to process data into tables and graphs for the final report
It is needed only if the teacher plans to mark the logbook for neatness
It provides an accurate, dated record that supports analysis, evaluation and honest reporting
It allows students to change data later if the results do not support the hypothesis
questions.explanation: A logbook is the primary record of what was done and observed, allowing results to be checked, errors traced and the method repeated. Altering data to fit a hypothesis is scientific misconduct.
